questions.q: Which city became the capital of unified Italy in 1871?
questions.explanation: Rome was annexed in 1870 and became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

questions.q: Otto von Bismarck was the chief minister of which state?
questions.explanation: Bismarck was the Prussian chief minister who led the unification of Germany.

questions.q: In which year was Greece recognised as an independent nation by the Treaty of Constantinople?
questions.explanation: The treaty of 1832 recognised Greece as independent.

questions.q: The print produced by Frederic Sorrieu in 1848 showed
options: a map of Italy at war
a dream of a world of democratic and social republics
questions.explanation: Sorrieu’s series of prints imagined peoples of Europe and America marching towards the Statue of Liberty.

questions.q: Why was Italy difficult to unify in the early nineteenth century?
options: It was divided into several states, and only one, Sardinia-Piedmont, was ruled by an Italian princely house
questions.explanation: Parts of Italy were under the Habsburgs, the Pope and the Bourbons, so unification required removing foreign rule.

questions.q: Why is it significant that women were only allowed to attend the Frankfurt Parliament as observers?
options: Women were the majority of members
It shows that women who had been active in the movement were denied political rights
It shows women chaired the meeting
It shows the Parliament was for women only
questions.explanation: Although many women took part in the liberal movement, they were not given the vote or membership.

questions.q: What was the July Revolution of 1830 in France?
questions.answer: A revolt in Paris in 1830 overthrew the Bourbon king who had been restored in 1815. Liberal revolutionaries installed a constitutional monarchy headed by Louis Philippe. It encouraged risings elsewhere, such as Belgium’s break from the Netherlands.
questions.explanation: The revolution showed that conservative order was not secure.

questions.q: Contrast the processes by which Italy and Germany became nation-states.
questions.answer: Italy’s unification involved the diplomacy of Cavour, the action of Garibaldi’s volunteers and the leadership of the king of Sardinia-Piedmont. Germany’s was led by Prussia under Bismarck through a series of wars. In both, a monarchy and an army, rather than liberal revolutions, achieved unification.
keyPoints: Germany: Prussia and Bismarck through wars
Both led by monarchies and armies
questions.explanation: Both unifications were led by strong states.

questions.q: Who is known as the ‘Frontier Gandhi’?
questions.explanation: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, a leader of the North-West Frontier, was known as the Frontier Gandhi.

questions.q: Who led the Indian National Army, or Azad Hind Fauj, during the Second World War?
questions.explanation: Subhas Chandra Bose organised and led the Indian National Army.

questions.q: Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali were prominent leaders of the
questions.explanation: The Ali brothers were leaders of the Khilafat Movement.

questions.q: Under Gandhiji’s leadership the national movement broadened its base by including
options: peasants, tribals, women and workers as well as the middle classes
questions.explanation: Gandhiji’s campaigns drew in groups that had earlier been outside the movement.

questions.q: Why did Muslim participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement remain lower than in the Khilafat days?
options: Muslims were not allowed to join
Muslims had no interest in freedom
After the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance faded, communal tensions grew and there were differences over political representation
questions.explanation: Communal tensions and disputes over representation weakened the earlier unity.

questions.q: Why did the Quit India Movement see widespread spontaneous protests?
options: Most leaders were arrested early, so ordinary people took the initiative
questions.explanation: With the leadership jailed, people across the country carried on protests on their own.

questions.q: Describe the participation of women in the Civil Disobedience Movement.
questions.answer: Thousands of women took part in protest marches, manufactured salt, picketed shops selling foreign cloth and liquor, and went to jail. Most were from high-caste families in towns or from rich peasant families in the countryside.
questions.explanation: Women’s participation was large, though they were mostly not in leadership roles.

questions.q: How did Gandhiji turn the national movement into a mass movement?
questions.answer: He used simple methods such as non-violent satyagraha, supported local struggles at Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad, linked different groups through issues like the Khilafat and the salt tax, and used symbols like khadi and the charkha that ordinary people understood.
keyPoints: Local struggles in Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad
Simple symbols such as khadi and salt
questions.explanation: Gandhiji connected the movement to everyday concerns.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The World Bank was originally set up mainly to
options: finance the post-war reconstruction of Europe
questions.explanation: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development was created to finance rebuilding of war-damaged Europe.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which of these was a member of the Central Powers in the First World War?
questions.explanation: Germany and Austria-Hungary were the main Central Powers.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: What fuelled the consumer boom in the USA in the 1920s?
options: Mass production of goods such as cars, refrigerators and radios, often bought on credit
questions.explanation: Mass production lowered prices and instalment buying spread, but it also left households in debt.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which Indian crop’s price fell sharply during the Great Depression, badly hitting farmers in Bengal?
questions.explanation: Jute prices collapsed, and growers fell deeply into debt.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Why did the Depression worsen when banks failed after 1929?
options: Credit dried up, so people and firms could not spend, which reduced demand and production
questions.explanation: Bank failures wiped out savings and stopped lending, deepening the fall in demand.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did the partition of Africa by European powers in the late nineteenth century affect Africans?
options: It gave Africans full control of resources
It drew colonial boundaries with little regard for local peoples and gave colonial rulers control over resources and labour
It made Africa a part of Asia
questions.explanation: At the Berlin conference of 1884–85, European powers divided Africa among themselves.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did Indian traders and bankers such as the Shikarpuri shroffs and Chettiars help international trade?
questions.answer: They financed agricultural exports from India and lent money to farmers and traders in Central and Southeast Asia. They also had their own methods of transferring money over long distances without physically moving cash.
keyPoints: Financed exports and trade in Central and Southeast Asia
Used their own system of transferring money
questions.explanation: Indian bankers were active in Asian trade.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did the Great Depression affect India?
questions.answer: India’s exports and imports fell sharply, and prices of agricultural goods such as jute and wheat dropped. Peasants who had to pay fixed revenue and had borrowed money were deeply indebted, and many were forced to sell land or jewellery.
questions.explanation: The slump in prices hit India’s farmers most.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Which two materials were basic to Britain’s early industrial growth?
questions.explanation: Coal and iron were key to making machines, steam power and railways.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: By the early twentieth century, which Indian city had become the largest centre of cotton mills?
questions.explanation: Bombay was the leading centre of the cotton textile industry.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why was the East India Company interested in Indian textiles in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries?
options: Fine Indian cotton and silk were in great demand in Europe
It wanted to stop all trade
It had no use for cloth
questions.explanation: Indian fine cloth was valued in European markets.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did Indian industrialists favour tariffs on imported cloth?
options: To protect Indian industry from competition from imports
questions.explanation: Tariffs made imports costlier, protecting local producers.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did Indian mills mostly produce coarse cotton yarn in their early years?
options: Yarn could be sold to handloom weavers and exported, while competing with fine British cloth was difficult
questions.explanation: Producing coarse yarn was easier and had markets at home and abroad.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did some fine handloom weaves, such as Banarasi saris, survive despite mill competition?
options: Mills could not imitate fine and intricate designs that rich buyers valued
questions.explanation: Intricate hand-woven designs were hard for mills to copy.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Give two differences between a cottage industry and a factory.
questions.answer: A cottage industry works at home or in small workshops with simple tools and family labour, producing in small quantities. A factory uses machines and many wage workers under one roof and produces in large quantities.
keyPoints: Cottage: home, simple tools, family labour, small scale
Factory: machines, wage workers, large scale
questions.explanation: The difference lies in scale, tools and organisation of work.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did weavers in Bengal often come into conflict with the Company’s gomasthas?
questions.answer: Gomasthas were outsiders who behaved arrogantly, punished weavers for delays in delivery and prevented them from selling to other buyers. Weavers who took advances had to hand over cloth at low prices, so many left their villages or resisted.
keyPoints: Gomasthas were outsiders and acted harshly
Weavers could not sell to others
Low prices; some weavers fled or rebelled
questions.explanation: The Company’s system reduced weavers’ independence.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: In which year was the Bengal Gazette first published?
questions.explanation: James Augustus Hickey started the Bengal Gazette in 1780.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Who started the journal Sambad Kaumudi?
questions.explanation: Raja Ram Mohan Roy started Sambad Kaumudi in 1821.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Gutenberg’s printing press was developed from
questions.explanation: Gutenberg adapted the screw press used for wine and olives.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: The Deoband seminary, founded in 1867, used print to
options: publish fatwas telling Muslims how to conduct themselves
questions.explanation: Deoband used print to spread religious guidance.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did newspapers and pamphlets in many languages help to build a shared sense of nationhood in India?
options: They spread nationalist ideas and made people feel part of one community
They were all written in one language
questions.explanation: Print created a shared body of ideas across regions.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Why were some people in eighteenth-century Europe worried about the spread of novels?
options: They feared that novels would encourage idleness and fantasy, especially among young readers and women
questions.explanation: Critics feared that fiction would distract readers from duties and lead them astray.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How were books produced in India before the coming of print?
questions.answer: Books were handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and regional languages, on palm leaves or handmade paper. They were costly and fragile, and their circulation was limited.
keyPoints: On palm leaf or handmade paper
questions.explanation: Copying by hand made books scarce.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did print affect books and reading in India’s regional languages in the nineteenth century?
questions.answer: Print made it possible to publish religious texts, novels, newspapers and translations cheaply in regional languages. New literary forms such as the novel developed, and more people, including women and the lower classes, began to read.
keyPoints: New forms such as the novel
questions.explanation: Print widened access to reading.

questions.q: Which of the following is a human-made resource?
questions.explanation: Roads, buildings and machines are human-made.

questions.q: The most widespread soil in India is
questions.explanation: Alluvial soil covers a large part of the northern plains and coastal areas.

questions.q: Net sown area is
options: the land on which crops are sown and harvested in a year
questions.explanation: Net sown area is the area actually cropped during the year.

questions.q: Planting rows of trees to break the force of the wind in dry areas is called
questions.explanation: Shelter belts protect the soil and help stabilise sand dunes.

questions.q: Why is a smaller share of land cultivated in hilly regions?
options: Steep slopes, thin soil and cold climates limit farming
questions.explanation: Relief and climate are physical limits to cultivation.

questions.q: Why is overgrazing a cause of land degradation in Rajasthan and Gujarat?
options: Grazing animals remove the vegetation, leaving the soil bare and exposed to wind
questions.explanation: Without plant cover, soil is easily blown away.

questions.q: State three features of alluvial soil.
questions.answer: Alluvial soil is deposited by rivers, is fertile and fine-grained, and contains potash and lime. It is found in the northern plains and in river deltas and is good for wheat, rice and sugarcane.
questions.explanation: Alluvial soil supports intensive farming.

questions.q: Why is the equitable distribution of resources necessary for sustainable life?
questions.answer: If resources are concentrated in few hands, many people are deprived, which causes conflict and hardship. Equitable distribution ensures everyone meets basic needs and prevents over-exploitation, which supports sustainable development.
questions.explanation: Fair sharing underpins sustainability.

questions.q: Which of these is a fibre crop?
questions.explanation: Cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk are fibre crops.

questions.q: Jowar, bajra and ragi are
options: cash crops of the plantation type
questions.explanation: Millets are coarse grains that grow in drier regions.

questions.q: Sugarcane grows best in
options: a hot and humid climate with irrigation
questions.explanation: Sugarcane needs warm, humid weather and plenty of water.

questions.q: Ahars and pynes are traditional water-management systems of
questions.explanation: Ahars are catchment basins and pynes are channels that lead water to fields in South Bihar.

questions.q: Why is overuse of chemical fertilisers a concern?
options: It can pollute soil and water and harm long-term soil fertility
It reduces pests permanently with no effect on anything else
questions.explanation: Excess chemicals run off into water and degrade the soil.

questions.q: Why does rainfall strongly influence the cropping pattern?
options: Crops such as rice need heavy rain while millets can grow in dry areas, so crops are chosen to suit the rainfall
All crops need the same water
questions.explanation: Different crops have different water needs.

questions.q: Name the three cropping seasons of India and give one crop of each.
questions.answer: The rabi season, with crops like wheat; the kharif season, with crops like rice; and the zaid season, a short summer season, with crops like watermelon.
questions.explanation: Seasons depend on sowing and harvesting times.

questions.q: Why has the use of groundwater increased, and what are the problems that result?
questions.answer: Tube wells and pumps made groundwater easy to use, especially for irrigation. Over-extraction lowers the water table, dries wells and increases costs, and water scarcity grows.
keyPoints: Tube wells and pumps made it easy to extract
questions.explanation: Pumping faster than recharge is unsustainable.

questions.q: Which mineral is the chief raw material for cement?
questions.explanation: Limestone is the main raw material for cement.

questions.q: Solar photovoltaic cells convert
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells produce electricity directly from sunlight.

questions.q: Coal and petroleum are mostly found in which type of rocks?
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels formed from organic matter in sedimentary rocks.

questions.q: Natural gas is usually found along with
questions.explanation: Natural gas is often found with petroleum or in separate gas fields.

questions.q: Why are sugar mills usually located close to sugarcane fields?
options: Cane is bulky and loses its sucrose content if not crushed soon after harvesting
Cane can be stored for years
questions.explanation: Cane must be processed quickly, so mills are close to fields.

questions.q: Why is the iron and steel industry called a basic industry?
options: It makes no use of coal
Many other industries depend on its products as raw material or machinery
questions.explanation: Steel is used in machinery, construction and transport.

questions.q: State two uses of manganese.
questions.answer: Manganese is used in making steel and ferro-alloys, as it improves the strength of steel. It is also used in manufacturing bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.
questions.explanation: Manganese is an essential alloy mineral.

questions.q: Discuss one advantage and one concern of nuclear energy.
questions.answer: Nuclear power plants produce large amounts of electricity from small quantities of uranium or thorium and emit little carbon dioxide. Concerns include the risk of accidents and the problem of safely disposing of radioactive waste.
keyPoints: Large energy from small fuel, low carbon emissions
questions.explanation: Nuclear power has benefits and risks.

questions.q: The head of a Gram Panchayat is called the
questions.explanation: The elected head of a Gram Panchayat is the Sarpanch or Gram Pradhan.

questions.q: The Zila Parishad works at the
questions.explanation: The Zila Parishad is the district-level body of the Panchayati Raj.

questions.q: Which statement about languages in the Indian Constitution is correct?
options: Hindi is the only language allowed
The Constitution did not give any one language the status of national language
questions.explanation: Hindi is the official language, but the Constitution lists many languages and gives none the status of national language.

questions.q: Which body governs a big city in India?
questions.explanation: Big cities are governed by municipal corporations headed by a Mayor.

questions.q: Why does the Constitution give more powers to the Union government than to the states?
options: To keep a large and diverse country united, with residuary powers resting with the Union
questions.explanation: The framers wished to strengthen national unity in a diverse country.

questions.q: Why has India accepted many languages in administration and education?
options: To respect linguistic diversity and avoid conflicts like those of Sri Lanka
It wants one language for everyone immediately
questions.explanation: Recognising several languages has helped to keep the country united.

questions.q: Distinguish between a Municipal Corporation and a Municipality.
questions.answer: A Municipal Corporation governs a big city and is headed by an elected Mayor. A Municipality governs a smaller town and is headed by a chairperson. Both consist of elected councillors.
questions.explanation: Both are urban local governments of different scale.

questions.q: What problems do local governments in India face even after getting constitutional status?
questions.answer: State governments have often been slow to hand over powers and funds to local bodies, and regular meetings of gram sabhas are not always held. Without adequate money and authority, local governments cannot function effectively.
keyPoints: States slow to transfer powers and funds
questions.explanation: Constitutional status alone does not guarantee effective local government.

questions.q: In a democracy, the final decision-making power rests with
options: the elected representatives of the people
questions.explanation: Democracy means rule by people’s elected representatives.

questions.q: The list of persons who are eligible to vote in an area is called the
questions.explanation: The electoral roll lists all eligible voters.

questions.q: Why are some seats in the Lok Sabha reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
options: To ensure that these groups are represented in the legislature
To reduce the number of seats
To give them control of the army
questions.explanation: Reservation ensures that their voices are heard in the legislature.

questions.q: Dynastic succession in a political party means that
options: leaders are elected by all members every year
family members of leaders tend to get top positions in the party
all positions are decided by lottery
questions.explanation: Relatives of party leaders often get tickets and posts, which weakens internal democracy.

questions.q: Why is a democratic government considered legitimate?
options: Because it is the people’s own government and citizens feel they have a stake in it
questions.explanation: Legitimacy comes from the people’s participation in choosing their government.

questions.q: Why have women remained under-represented in many legislatures?
options: Women are not allowed to vote
There are no women in society
Social barriers and household responsibilities limit their participation, and parties often give them few tickets
questions.explanation: Customs, unequal division of work and party practices reduce women’s presence in politics.

questions.q: What is a coalition government?
questions.answer: It is a government formed by two or more political parties that join together when no single party has a majority of seats in the legislature. They agree on a common programme and share ministerial posts.
keyPoints: Formed by two or more parties
When no party has a majority
questions.explanation: Coalitions are common in multi-party systems.

questions.q: Suggest two reforms that could make Indian democracy stronger.
questions.answer: Political parties could hold regular internal elections and make their finances open to public scrutiny. Candidates should disclose their assets and criminal cases so that voters can make informed choices, and more women should be given tickets.
keyPoints: Internal democracy and transparency in parties
questions.explanation: Transparency and participation strengthen democracy.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: The average number of years a person is expected to live is called
questions.explanation: Life expectancy is a key indicator of health in the Human Development Index.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: The Public Distribution System provides
questions.explanation: The PDS supplies foodgrains such as rice, wheat and sugar to households at lower prices.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Cotton grown by farmers is used as raw material in
options: the cotton textile industry, a secondary sector activity
questions.explanation: The cotton textile industry is a secondary activity using a primary product.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Underemployment is a situation in which people
options: appear to be employed but are working less than their capacity
questions.explanation: People in underemployment do work but could produce more if fully employed.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why does the government set up public sector enterprises in backward regions?
options: To promote development in areas where private firms may not invest
questions.explanation: Public investment can bring jobs and infrastructure to neglected regions.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why must the environment be considered when judging development?
options: Because development that depletes resources and harms the environment cannot be sustained and harms future generations
questions.explanation: Sustainable development protects resources for the future.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Define GDP.
questions.answer: Gross Domestic Product is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.
keyPoints: Total value of final goods and services
questions.explanation: GDP measures the size of an economy’s output.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Explain with an example why averages like per capita income can be misleading when comparing development.
questions.answer: Two countries may have the same average income, but in one the income is shared fairly while in the other a few people are very rich and the rest are poor. The average does not show this inequality, nor does it tell about health, education or facilities.
keyPoints: Same average can hide unequal distribution
questions.explanation: Averages hide differences within a population.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: The World Trade Organization is
options: a body that gives loans to students
an organisation that sets rules for international trade
questions.explanation: The WTO sets rules for international trade and settles trade disputes.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: The Consumer Protection Act was passed in India in
questions.explanation: The Consumer Protection Act, 1986, set up the consumer commissions.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: The consumer’s ‘right to be heard’ means that
options: consumers’ interests will receive due consideration at appropriate forums
consumers may hear music in shops
questions.explanation: Consumers have the right to put their complaints and interests before suitable bodies.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: A fixed limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported is called a
questions.explanation: A quota is a limit on the quantity of imports.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why is it important that credit is available to the poor on reasonable terms?
options: It makes them borrow more than they need
It helps them to start or expand work and raise their income instead of falling into a debt trap
questions.explanation: Affordable credit allows the poor to invest in livelihoods.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why did the consumer movement develop in India?
options: To protect consumers against unfair practices such as adulteration, hoarding and black-marketing
questions.explanation: Consumers organised to resist exploitation by unscrupulous traders.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: How do multinational companies spread production across countries?
questions.answer: They set up factories or offices in different countries, often where costs are low or markets are large, or place orders with local producers. As a result, production is carried out across many countries.
keyPoints: Set up units in different countries
Choose low cost or big markets
questions.explanation: MNCs organise production on a global scale.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: What measures could make globalisation fairer?
questions.answer: Governments can enforce labour laws to protect workers, support small producers with credit and technology, and negotiate fair rules in international trade so that developing countries are not disadvantaged.
questions.explanation: Fair rules can spread the gains of globalisation.

questions.q: India became a republic on
questions.explanation: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, making India a republic.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: In which country did Gutenberg develop his printing press?
questions.explanation: Gutenberg worked in Strasbourg and Mainz in Germany.

questions.q: Who led the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928?
questions.explanation: Vallabhbhai Patel led the peasants’ satyagraha against the increase in land revenue at Bardoli.

questions.q: Which crop is the main raw material for the sugar industry?
questions.explanation: Sugar is manufactured from sugarcane.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Great Depression began in
questions.explanation: The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted into the mid-1930s.

questions.q: Which mineral is used as an alloy in making steel?
questions.explanation: Manganese is used in steel-making.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why are health and education important for human development?
questions.answer: A healthy and educated population can work more productively, earn more and live longer, and has better opportunities. They are basic needs that raise the quality of life, so they are included in measures such as the Human Development Index.
keyPoints: Included in the Human Development Index
questions.explanation: People’s capabilities are central to development.

questions.q: State two functions of the Election Commission of India.
questions.answer: The Election Commission prepares the electoral rolls and conducts elections to Parliament and State Legislatures. It also enforces the code of conduct and allots symbols to parties and candidates.
keyPoints: Prepares electoral rolls and conducts elections
Enforces the code of conduct or allots symbols
questions.explanation: It is an independent body for free and fair elections.
